thread.title: Apple: Where The Modern Corporation Is Going - II

author: John M. Mason
title: Apple: Where The Modern Corporation Is Going - II
text:
Two weeks ago I wrote about Apple, Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL ) as the “ Epitome of Where the Modern Corporation is Going .”
As Apple approaches a market cap of $1 trillion with a return on shareholder’s equity of 36.1 percent in 2017, it can be thought that Apple’s management is doing a lot of things right… enough things that other corporations should be following them.
And, what does Apple produce?
Apple produces iPhones and iPads and MacBooks. Right?
But, Apple does a lot more of this and appears to be on the leading edge of how modern corporations need to bring all that they do together in order to produce the results Apple does… and sustain them.
It turns out that Apple’s success is not just tied to the physical goods it produces. Oh, that is an important part of what they do, but they have gone beyond just the production of goods to show how, in this modern world of information technology, different facets of “information” can be tied together to make something really substantial…and really profitable.
Rana Foroohar, who writes for the Financial Times, claimed three talents , not connected directly with the production side of Apple, that helped to account for the outstanding performance of the company and why this company needs to be considered as a model corporation for the new era we are moving into.
First, Apple does produce very good products. We can start with that. And, with an ROE in excess of 20.0 percent for the last fifteen years or so, Apple is generating lots of cash!
Ms. Foroohar discusses how Apple uses financial engineering to manage its cash, debt, and other financial activities and then uses financial engineering to build its corporate structure through M&A.
Furthermore, both of these skills represent little more than being particularly adept with information, for finance, at its most basic level, is nothing more than information, zeros and ones.
In today’s world, where credit inflation is the fundamental environment corporations and others work within, excelling in financial engineering is a prime requirement for good financial results.
However, Ms. Foroohar also states that Apple is a leader in the use of intangibles like intellectual property and brands relative to tangible goods. She further emphasis the fact that especially intellectual property is extremely scalable and enjoys network effects.
As I wrote in my earlier post, “Information goods like these tend to have a zero or close to zero marginal cost, which allows a corporation to expand almost without constraint. A consequence of this is that corporations build along these blueprints do not spend, proportionately, as much on physical capital, and their output is less about the production of goods and more about the production and networking of information.”
And, this leads right into another fact that is contributing more and more to Apple’s overall performance. That is the contribution Apple’s services business.
Tim Bradshaw writes in the Financial Times about Apple’s “second-largest source of revenue…its services business composed of revenues from items like App Store downloads, iCloud storage and Apple Music subscriptions, among others.
These areas, altogether, “brought in more than $9 billion in the last quarter, up 31 percent on the year."
And, they are “a model of consistency compared with the feast-or-famine performance of the iPhone. Since 2006, it has grown at an average rate of 23 percent, year-on-year….”
“Services revenues have doubled in four years.”
Tim Cook, Apple CEO, and his CFO Luca Maestri, have gone on record as setting a target of $50 billion for the division by the end of 2020.
And, a $1 trillion market cap is not a small achievement, either.
The point is that Apple is creating the modern corporation and is showing others that it is not just the production of a product that is all that is needed.
The modern corporation must become an “information” corporation, one that thrives upon how production and production’s surrounding offerings can be combined in a way that optimizes the overall performance of the company.
And, this combination of “information goods” may not be initially obvious to those observing the construction of these organizations. Just look at what Amazon.com is doing. Look at what Alphabet, Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOG ) is doing. Look at what Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ) is doing. And, there are others.
The important thing is that these “modern” corporations are using “information” to tie all things together.
This is a giant step from another effort to build a business conglomerate that was not based on the integration of divisions based upon the connecting world of “information.”
The corporate conglomerate I am thinking of is General Electric (NYSE: GE ). Jack Welch attempted to bring many different companies and divisions together and run them out of a holding company like a financial portfolio of stocks. He even has substantial divisions that were purely of a financial nature and, at one time in the 1990s, General Electric generated more than 60 percent of its profits just from its financial divisions.
But, Mr. Welch was ahead of his time. Creating a portfolio of companies comparable to a portfolio of stocks was maybe consistent with current thinking at the time “Welch’s monstrosity” was constructed. The companies, however, were run as independent entities. There were scale and scope problems.
Jeff Immelt, who followed Mr. Welch into the leader’s position, spent a lot of his time undoing what his predecessor built. And, John Flannery, Mr. Welch’s successor, is spending a lot of his time trying to decide on how further downsizing of General Electric’s portfolio of companies is to take place.
The important takeaway from this is that the “newest” modern world is all about “information” and how “information” fits together.
The high-tech companies are building a new model and Apple, Inc. is one of the leaders here. The issue is not about how you put products together, it is not like constructing a portfolio of assets. The issue is, how do you build networks and how can networks scale and broaden scope? This is a completely different process.
